source.title: Biased online media coverage: chiropractic and stroke in google news

paper.citation: Al-Azdee, M., Perle, S. M., & He, B. (2018). Biased online media coverage: Chiropractic and stroke in Google News. Chiropractic & Manual Therapies, 26, 21. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12998-018-0189-8
paper.abstract: How many Google News texts in 2015 linked chiropractic treatment and stroke-related terms, where were they ranked, and how were their tones classified? The unit of analysis was 146 Google News texts from 2015, not patients, athletes, or clinical outcomes. The study concerns media framing of chiropractic and stroke; it does not estimate stroke risk after manipulation. Relevance to sport performance is limited to critical appraisal and risk communication. Quantitative content analysis using seven keyword frames across the first 10 Google News result pages for January–December 2015. One primary coder classified 12 categorical variables; a second coder independently coded 10% of texts, with reported absolute agreement. Descriptive prevalence and likelihood-ratio tests were used.
paper.tldr: This content-analysis study is indirectly relevant to evidence communication: it shows how search framing, tone coding, and platform ranking can shape perceptions of a contested health-risk claim. The search yielded 146 texts; 35% appeared on the first Google News results page and 65% on later pages. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Quantitative content analysis using seven keyword frames across the first 10 Google News result pages for January–December 2015. One primary coder classified 12 categorical variables; a second coder independently coded 10% of texts, with reported absolute agreement. Descriptive prevalence and likelihood-ratio tests were used.
paper.findings: The search yielded 146 texts; 35% appeared on the first Google News results page and 65% on later pages. Ninety-five percent were classified as negative overall: 20% "negative" and 75% "negative connotation"; 5% were positive and none neutral under the study's coding rules. The coding definition treated mentioning the alleged causal relation without arguing for or against it as negative connotation, so the headline 95% figure partly reflects an a priori classification choice. The study measured text counts and placement, not impressions, audience beliefs, behavior, or clinical consequences.
paper.limitations: Data covered only one calendar year and one platform. Google News ranking is dynamic, personalized, and algorithm-dependent; the paper's results are a historical snapshot. A single primary coder classified all items, and the reliability subsample was only 15 texts. The study could not track impressions or duplicated wire-service reach across outlets. Its framing assumes the causal relation is unverified and defines neutral mention as negative connotation; readers should separate that operational definition from an independent assessment of clinical evidence.
paper.practicalImplications: Use this paper as a reminder to audit how risk messages are sampled and coded. When communicating athlete-health evidence, separate event incidence, causal certainty, and media tone; document search dates and ranking context; and avoid treating search-result prevalence as a proxy for clinical risk or public exposure.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use this paper as a reminder to audit how risk messages are sampled and coded. When communicating athlete-health evidence, separate event incidence, causal certainty, and media tone; document search dates and ranking context; and avoid treating search-result prevalence as a proxy for clinical risk or public exposure. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
